strengths: Introduces HydraFake, a well-constructed and thoughtfully designed hierarchical benchmark (In-Domain/Cross-Model/Cross-Forgery/Cross-Domain) that better reflects real-world deployment challenges than the standard FF++-based protocol; the dataset covers diverse and up-to-date forgery techniques (VAR models, personalization, relighting, restoration, generative swapping, in-the-wild social media data) with careful quality control.

The pattern-aware reasoning framework (fast judgement, planning, reasoning, self-reflection, conclusion) is a reasonable and well-motivated adaptation of human forensic reasoning to deepfake detection, and is shown empirically to outperform vanilla CoT and post-hoc explanation baselines (Table 2).

The two-stage training pipeline (SFT cold-start + MiPO + P-GRPO) is methodologically sound and includes a novel Mixed Preference Optimization strategy and pattern-aware reward design tailored to encourage useful self-reflection/planning while penalizing overthinking that leads to wrong answers.

Extensive experiments: comparisons against 10 SOTA detectors and 6 MLLMs (including GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Pro), thorough ablations on training stages, reward components, base model choice/size, robustness to compression/blur, and both automatic (score/ELO) and qualitative reasoning-quality evaluations.

Results show substantial and consistent gains over baselines, especially in the more challenging cross-forgery and cross-domain OOD settings which is exactly where the paper claims existing methods fail, supporting the central thesis of the work.
Good transparency/reproducibility effort: detailed dataset construction, full annotation prompts, and full per-subset breakdown tables provided in appendix.
weaknesses: The dataset construction involves substantial manual curation, filtering, and multiple proprietary/commercial data sources (Adobe Firefly, StarryAI, social media crawling with watermark removal), raising reproducibility and potential licensing/ethics concerns that are only briefly addressed in the Ethics Statement.

Reliance on MLLM-based automated annotation (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Qwen3-235B, ensemble voting) for constructing the SFT/MiPO training data introduces a risk of inherited biases or errors from the annotator models propagating into VERITAS's reasoning, which is not deeply analyzed (e.g., no human validation accuracy rate reported for the annotation pipeline).

Performance on Cross-Domain low-resolution/legacy subsets (e.g., DeepFaceLab, FFIW) remains weak and even lower than several baselines in Precision (Table 11), suggesting the model's gains are somewhat concentrated in high-resolution/OOD generative scenarios rather than uniformly across all challenge types, which tempers the generality claims.

The reward design (pattern-aware reward, reflection quality reward via an external MLLM judge) has several hand-tuned hyperparameters (e.g., specific reward magnitudes in Eq. 5) without much sensitivity analysis or justification for the specific values chosen.

Comparisons to closed reasoning-capable baselines (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro) rely on prompting without any fine-tuning, which is an expected but somewhat unfair comparison given VERITAS is extensively fine-tuned on the exact training distribution used for evaluation splits; a fine-tuned/few-shot version of a comparable closed model could be a stronger, though harder-to-obtain, comparison.

Given the specialized in-domain training data (facial deepfakes) and the relatively narrow definition of 'domain', the claimed generalization to truly novel/unanticipated deepfake types (beyond the curated hierarchical splits) remains somewhat speculative; robustness against actively adversarial or evolving forgery methods not represented in the taxonomy is untested.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap in the deepfake-detection literature: existing benchmarks (train on FF++, test on a handful of old datasets) do not reflect real-world diversity of generators and domains. HydraFake's hierarchical protocol (in-domain / cross-model / cross-forgery / cross-domain) is a useful organizing framework for the community.

Extensive empirical comparison against 10 SOTA detectors and 6 open/closed-source MLLMs across 19 subsets, with Accuracy/Precision/Recall reported for every subset in the appendix, giving a reasonably thorough empirical picture.

Reasonably detailed ablations isolating the contribution of SFT, MiPO and P-GRPO stages, different reward terms (pattern-aware reward, reflection-quality reward, format reward), and different base models/sizes.

The two-stage pipeline (cold-start SFT + MiPO, followed by pattern-aware GRPO) is a sensible combination of existing techniques (DPO-style alignment + RLVR) adapted with a task-specific reward design, and the paper reports consistent gains over vanilla CoT and vanilla GRPO in controlled comparisons.
Reasonable robustness checks (JPEG compression, Gaussian blur) and reasoning-quality evaluation via LLM-as-judge/ELO, going beyond simple accuracy.
weaknesses: Potential data leakage / overlap of generation pipelines between training and evaluation splits is not clearly ruled out: several of the "unseen" cross-forgery/cross-domain generators (e.g., InfiniteYou appears in both Cross-Forgery and Cross-Domain splits, PuLID/InfiniteYou personalization reuse the same FFHQ source images as training) share considerable methodological similarity with in-domain or other test subsets, which could inflate apparent generalization and undercuts the claimed novelty of the "hierarchical OOD" design.

The SFT/MiPO reasoning data is itself generated almost entirely by an ensemble of MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Qwen3-235B, InternVL3-78B) with only light human verification (3K MiPO pairs manually curated out of 36K+ SFT samples); there is no systematic human audit of hallucination rates in the "factual" reasoning traces used for training, despite hallucination being a well-known MLLM failure mode directly relevant to this task.

The qualitative examples presented throughout the paper (Fig. 1, 8–13) are cherry-picked success cases, and several of the "forensic" claims in the reasoning traces (e.g., "unnatural fabric texture," "badge text lacks alignment," "overly smooth skin lacking imperfections") are generic/vague post-hoc rationalizations that are difficult to verify as causally linked to the model's actual decision — the paper's own reward design explicitly penalizes such vague statements, yet the qualitative examples still contain them.

Despite claims of "significant gains," several evaluation subsets remain weak (e.g., DeepFaceLab accuracy 58.6%, IC-Light relighting 75.7%, where a baseline CNN detector (Effort) clearly outperforms VERITAS), and the paper does not provide a convincing analysis or fix for these systematic failure modes beyond a brief post-hoc explanation.

The reflection-quality and pattern-aware reward functions rely on an auxiliary MLLM judge (UnifiedReward-Qwen-3B) and GPT-4o/Gemini-2.5-Pro as evaluators; using LLM-as-judge for both the reward signal during training and the downstream quality evaluation introduces a risk of circularity/self-reinforcing bias that is not discussed or controlled for.

Key implementation details (λ1, λ2 reward weighting, how 'planning'/'reflection' presence P, R are detected programmatically, full MiPO/P-GRPO hyperparameters) are under-specified in the main text, limiting reproducibility.

The core architectural/training contribution is an aggregation of fairly standard existing techniques (SFT cold-start, DPO-style preference optimization relabeled as MiPO, GRPO with custom reward shaping) applied to a new domain; the technical novelty beyond dataset curation and reward engineering is incremental.

No video-level or temporal evaluation despite including video-based forgery sources (MAGI-1, Hailuo AI), only sampling frames, which may not adequately test genuinely video-specific artifacts that differ from static image forensics.

Claims of being "the first attempt to introduce human-like reasoning into deepfake detection" are overstated given concurrently cited works (FakeReasoning, Mirage, AIGI-Holmes) already explore reasoning-based AIGC/deepfake detection; the distinction drawn (facial-specific, adaptive patterns) is somewhat thin.

strengths: The HydraFake-100K dataset addresses a genuine and important gap in deepfake detection research: existing benchmarks poorly reflect practical deployment conditions (narrow training sources, limited and low-resolution testing). The hierarchical protocol (in-domain, cross-model, cross-forgery, cross-domain) with carefully curated real-world forgery types (VAR architectures, face relighting, personalization, restoration, generative swapping, social-media in-the-wild samples from commercial apps) is a valuable and timely resource for the community.

The pattern-aware reasoning framework is a well-motivated and reasonably novel contribution, moving beyond vanilla CoT and post-hoc explanation paradigms toward reasoning that is causally tied to the final decision (formalized clearly in Appendix A.2), which is conceptually sound and distinguishes the work from prior MLLM-based explainable deepfake detectors that rely on small vision models for the final classification.

The two-stage training pipeline (SFT cold-start + MiPO, followed by P-GRPO with a custom pattern-aware reward) is technically detailed and supported by thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each component (Table 2, Table 3, Figure 5, Figure 6), showing consistent and non-trivial gains, particularly on OOD splits.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: comparisons against 10 SOTA detectors and 6 MLLMs/closed-source models, full per-subset breakdowns with precision/recall in the appendix, reasoning-quality evaluation via independent LLM judges and ELO ratings, and robustness tests under compression/blur, which collectively provide convincing evidence for the claimed improvements.

The paper is transparent about dataset construction, quality control, and annotation pipeline (including prompts in the appendix), aiding reproducibility and providing useful qualitative examples that illustrate both successes and the effect of individual components (e.g., MiPO vs. no-MiPO in Figure 1).
weaknesses: Despite strong averages, VERITAS still performs poorly on several individual cross-domain subsets (e.g., ~58.6% on DeepFaceLab, barely above chance), and the paper's emphasis on aggregate SOTA gains somewhat obscures these persistent failure modes; a more explicit discussion of when and why the method fails would strengthen the claims.

The MiPO preference dataset relies on 3K human-annotated preference pairs, but details on annotator qualifications, inter-annotator agreement, and annotation cost/time are largely missing, raising reproducibility concerns for this costly component.

The reflection-quality reward and much of the SFT data rely on model-based judgments (UnifiedReward-Qwen-3B, GPT-4o/Gemini as judges, Qwen/Kimi/InternVL voting for artifact selection), which risks compounding biases or hallucinated artifact explanations into the training signal; the reliability of these automated judges is not independently validated against human forensic experts.

There is no direct human evaluation of the faithfulness/trustworthiness of the generated reasoning traces beyond automated LLM-as-judge scoring, which may not fully capture whether the explanations are causally grounded in genuine artifacts versus plausible-sounding rationalizations.

Practical deployment considerations such as inference latency/cost of the heavy multi-pattern reasoning process (versus small vision-model baselines) are not discussed, despite the paper's motivation being closing the gap to industrial practice.

Some cross-forgery/cross-domain generalization claims could be inflated by the fact that several "unseen" techniques still share underlying generative architectures (e.g., diffusion-based EFG in training vs. diffusion-based novel forgeries in testing), warranting more careful disentanglement of true architectural novelty versus superficial unseen branding.

Given that the dataset includes proprietary/commercial-app-generated content (GPT-4o, Dreamina, Hailuo AI) and social-media-crawled images, there could be redistribution/licensing constraints affecting the dataset's long-term reproducibility and community reuse.

strengths: Introduces HydraFake, a well-constructed dataset with a hierarchical evaluation protocol (in-domain, cross-model, cross-forgery, cross-domain) that more realistically reflects industrial deployment challenges than the standard FF++-to-other-datasets protocol, covering diverse forgery types (FS, FR, EFG, relighting, restoration, personalization, VAR-based generation) and in-the-wild social media data.

Proposes a well-motivated pattern-aware reasoning framework (fast judgement, planning, reasoning, self-reflection, conclusion) grounded in human forensic analysis, with a thoughtfully designed two-stage training pipeline (SFT cold-start + MiPO + P-GRPO) to instill this reasoning into MLLMs.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: comparisons against 10 SOTA small-vision detectors, 6 generic MLLMs, and 5 MLLM-based forgery detectors, plus thorough ablations on reasoning patterns, training stages, reward components, hyperparameters, reward models, and cross-benchmark generalization (AIGIBench, LOKI, FakeClue, Forensics-Bench, Nano-banana).

Strong empirical results: significant gains on cross-forgery and cross-domain OOD scenarios (previously a major weakness of existing detectors), and demonstrated generalization to broader AIGC detection benchmarks despite training only on facial data, indicating the reasoning-based approach transfers well beyond the exact training distribution.

High transparency and reproducibility efforts: detailed appendix with full data construction pipeline, all prompt templates, extensive qualitative case studies, failure analysis, and honest discussion of limitations (e.g., low-resolution image struggles, image-only scope).
weaknesses: The MiPO preference data (3K samples) and part of the SFT annotation pipeline rely on manual/human curation and multi-step MLLM annotation pipelines that may be difficult to scale or fully reproduce without the exact annotation infrastructure and human annotators used by the authors.

Reasoning quality evaluation relies on MLLM-as-a-judge (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro) and a learned reward model for reflection quality, which could introduce evaluator bias or reward hacking that is not fully explored (e.g., no human evaluation cross-check reported for the reasoning quality claims in Table 7).

Despite strong average gains, performance on some cross-domain subsets remains weak (e.g., DeepFaceLab accuracy is only 58.6%, lower than several baselines), and the paper's explanation for this (low precision on unseen low-resolution real images) suggests a persisting core weakness not fully solved by the proposed method.

The efficiency/inference-time cost of the multi-stage pattern-aware reasoning (particularly under P-GRPO) versus simpler classifiers is non-trivial for practical deployment, and while an efficiency analysis is provided, the trade-off between accuracy gains and inference latency on high-resolution images could be discussed more critically in the main text rather than solely in the appendix.

strengths: Introduces HydraFake, a well-motivated benchmark with a hierarchical OOD evaluation protocol (in-domain/cross-model/cross-forgery/cross-domain) that addresses genuine limitations of the standard FF++-to-others protocol used in prior deepfake detection work.

Extensive experimental comparisons against a large number of baselines: 10 small vision-model detectors, several generic MLLMs, and multiple MLLM-based forgery detectors, providing a fairly comprehensive empirical picture.

The two-stage training pipeline (SFT cold-start, MiPO preference alignment, and Pattern-aware GRPO) is a reasonably novel combination that yields consistent gains over ablated variants (Tables 2, 3, 6, Figure 4/5).

Substantial ablation and analysis effort: reward component ablations, hyperparameter studies, reasoning pattern ablations, efficiency analysis, cross-benchmark generalization (AIGIBench, LOKI, FakeClue, Forensics-Bench, Nano-banana), and failure case analysis.
Reasonably transparent documentation of the data annotation pipeline, prompts, and design choices in the appendix, aiding reproducibility understanding.
weaknesses: The 'pattern-aware reasoning' taxonomy (fast/planning/reasoning/reflection/conclusion) is a hand-designed heuristic without principled justification for why this specific decomposition is necessary or optimal versus other reasoning structures; the ablations show some patterns (e.g., 'fast') contribute little.

The reward design in P-GRPO (Rpattern with hard-coded values 2.0/1.0/-0.5/-1.0, format rewards, reflection-quality reward from an auxiliary 3B model) is heavily hand-engineered with limited theoretical grounding and only coarse sensitivity analysis; the 'novelty of reflection' criterion judged by a small VLM is not rigorously validated as reliable.

Since the same team constructs both the benchmark (HydraFake) and the detection model (VERITAS), there is inherent risk of the evaluation protocol and data curation choices (e.g., what counts as 'seen'/'unseen', selection of subsets, quality filtering) being implicitly tuned to favor the proposed pipeline, which cross-benchmark results only partially mitigate.

Performance remains weak on several practically important subsets (e.g., DeepFaceLab in cross-domain at 58.6%, low precision on several low-resolution real subsets), undermining the claim of robust generalization; the model still fails in ways similar to baselines on low-quality/low-resolution content.

The data annotation pipeline for SFT/MiPO relies on cascades of multiple large proprietary/open models (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Qwen3-235B-A22B, InternVL3-78B, Kimi-VL) plus manual human curation (3K MiPO pairs), making the pipeline expensive, complex, and difficult to reproduce faithfully.

Claims of 'human-aligned' and 'forensic-expert-like' reasoning are somewhat overstated; the reasoning traces are shaped by reward-driven RL optimization for verifiable answers rather than demonstrated causal/faithful reasoning, and the paper's own failure analysis and inconsistent case studies (e.g., Figure 20/22) suggest the produced explanations can still be superficial or misleading despite correct answers.

Efficiency/practicality trade-offs versus lightweight CNN-based detectors are not deeply analyzed in terms of deployment cost despite the practical framing of the paper (industrial deployment motivation in the introduction).

The work is restricted to single-frame facial images; video deepfakes, which are explicitly noted as an important real-world threat in the introduction, are left entirely unaddressed, weakening the practical significance claims.

strengths: Introduces HydraFake, a hierarchical benchmark (in-domain, cross-model, cross-forgery, cross-domain) that addresses a genuine gap between academic deepfake detection protocols and real-world industrial scenarios with abundant but narrow training sources and diverse test-time forgeries.

The pattern-aware reasoning framework (fast judgement, planning, reasoning, reflection, conclusion) is well-motivated by human forensic processes and is empirically validated against flexible CoT and post-hoc explanation baselines (Table 2, Table 5).

The two-stage training pipeline (SFT cold-start + Mixed Preference Optimization + Pattern-aware GRPO) is a thoughtful combination of techniques tailored to the specific challenges of deepfake reasoning (sparse semantics, low-level artifacts), with strong ablations showing each stage's contribution (Figure 4, Figure 5, Table 6).

Extensive comparisons across small vision models, generic MLLMs, and MLLM-based forgery detectors, plus cross-benchmark generalization tests (AIGIBench, LOKI, FakeClue, Forensics-Bench, Nano-banana) that demonstrate the method generalizes beyond the paper's own benchmark.
Thorough ablation studies on reward function components, hyperparameters (β', G), reward models, and P-GRPO training data selection, going well beyond what is typical for a submission.
Honest discussion of limitations, failure cases, and efficiency trade-offs, plus detailed appendix with full prompts and data construction pipeline that aids reproducibility.
Robustness evaluation under compression/blur perturbations shows the model generalizes without being explicitly trained with such augmentations, unlike prior methods.
weaknesses: Performance on several cross-domain low-resolution subsets (e.g., DeepFaceLab, FFIW) remains weak (Precision issues), indicating the method's core limitation on lower-quality data is not fully resolved despite strong gains elsewhere.

The SFT training data is annotated via an ensemble of other MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Kimi-VL, InternVL3-78B, Qwen3-235B) rather than human experts for most samples; systematic biases or errors in this teacher ensemble could propagate into the model's learned reasoning patterns, and this is only partially mitigated by the small (3K) human-curated MiPO set.

The reward model for reflection quality (UnifiedReward-Qwen-3B) is itself an MLLM-based scorer, introducing another layer of potential noise/bias into the RL reward signal that is not deeply analyzed beyond a coarse reward-model ablation.
The overall pipeline (SFT + MiPO + P-GRPO with multiple specialized rewards) is fairly complex, which may pose reproducibility/engineering barriers for others despite prompts being provided.
The method is restricted to single-image inputs; video-based deepfakes (a growing real-world threat) are explicitly left to future work, limiting immediate practical scope.

Some baseline comparisons (e.g., MLLM-based detectors) are evaluated zero-shot or with limited-scope training (VERITAS-MINI) for fairness, but the exact match in training data quantity/distribution across all baselines is not always perfectly controlled, leaving some residual uncertainty in fairness of comparisons.
